name: Vachaspati-Vilenkin Wiggly Cosmic String
description: The averaged gravitational field of a cosmic string carrying small waves. Its energy per length exceeds its tension, and the averaged geometry attracts matter initially at rest.
convention: We use $G=c=1$, with energy per length $U$ and tension $T$ in geometrical units. The tensors are exact tensors of the truncated line element; the vacuum field equations hold through first order in $U$ and $T$. The Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu}=R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.
history: Small waves on a cosmic string change its averaged gravitational field. At distances large compared with the waves, the averaged string has an energy per length $U$ and a tension $T$ [campsemparan2010]. Brandon Carter described the averaged string by an elastic model in 1990, with the equation of state $UT=\mu_0^2$ [carter1990noisy]. Here $\mu_0$ is the energy per length and tension of the unperturbed string. Alexander Vilenkin derived the same equation of state that year for short waves on the string, by a different method [vilenkin1990].¶Writing $U=\alpha\mu_0$, where $\alpha>1$ measures the excess energy, fixes $T=\mu_0/\alpha$. Hence $U-T=\mu_0(\alpha-\alpha^{-1})>0$. A straight string has its energy per length equal to its tension. The exterior is locally flat, with a conical deficit about the axis, and matter initially at rest feels no gravitational attraction [campsemparan2010].¶Tanmay Vachaspati and Vilenkin solved the linearized Einstein equations for the averaged string in 1991 [vachaspativilenkin1991]. The two quantities $U$ and $T$ determine its gravitational field to first order in the gravitational coupling [campsemparan2010]. For the averaged wiggly string the difference $U-T$ is positive, so the Newtonian gravitational potential varies with distance from the axis [campsemparan2010]. In units $G=c=1$, the Newtonian potential is $\Phi=2(U-T)\ln(r/r_0)$, where $r$ is distance from the axis and $r_0$ is a reference length [campsemparan2010]. Matter released from rest has the inward radial acceleration $d^2r/dt^2=-2(U-T)/r$ to first order. For a straight string $U=T$, and that acceleration vanishes.¶Vachaspati and Vilenkin showed that wakes behind wiggly strings could produce cosmic structure and large streaming velocities and leave the microwave background nearly uniform [vachaspativilenkin1991]. A string moving at speed $v_s$, with Lorentz factor $\gamma_s$, gives matter beside its path a velocity kick $2\pi(U-T)/(\gamma_s v_s)+4\pi U v_s\gamma_s$ toward the plane it sweeps, the first term from the Newtonian attraction and the second from the conical deficit [perivolaropoulos2005]. Vachaspati solved for the fluid flow in these wakes in 1992 and found strong shocks after recombination, with vortical flow behind them that generates a magnetic field [vachaspati1992]. Dan N. Vollick computed the response of cold dark matter to a network of wiggly strings the same year and found wakes that may account for the observed large scale structure, together with large peculiar velocities [vollick1992].¶Anthony N. Aguirre and Robert H. Brandenberger treated a slowly moving wiggly string as a Newtonian line source of density $U-T$ in 1995 and found that hot dark matter collapses onto it into filaments that go nonlinear before redshift 100 [aguirrebrandenberger1995]. Brandenberger and coauthors extended the calculation to moving strings in 1996, and the first filaments of hot dark matter still formed near redshift 100 [zanchinlimabrandenberger1996]. Pedro F. González-Díaz and José A. Jiménez Madrid computed the accretion of dark energy onto the string through this geometry in 2006 [gonzalezdiazjimenezmadrid2006]. Dark energy with pressure $p=w\rho$ and $w>-1$ raises $U$ toward a finite maximum, and phantom energy, with $w<-1$, lowers it back to $\mu_0$ and leaves a string without waves [gonzalezdiazjimenezmadrid2006].¶Jooyoo Hong, Jaewan Kim, and Pierre Sikivie confirmed the equation of state at lowest order in 1992 and found that it fails at fourth order in the wave amplitude once longitudinal waves are present [hongkimsikivie1992]. Kim and Sikivie showed in 1994 that $UT=\mu_0^2$ is a fixed point of the averaging at lowest order, however many generations of waves are averaged out [kimsikivie1994]. Xavier Martin showed in 1995 that the higher order corrections cancel exactly when the energy of a wiggly segment is divided by the straight distance between its ends [martin1995, carter1995]. Carter proved the same year that the transonic model, in which transverse and longitudinal waves share the speed $\sqrt{T/U}$, follows a wiggly Nambu-Goto worldsheet without accumulating error as long as the string does not cross itself [carter1995]. Carter found in 1999 that the gravitational interaction of an elastic string with itself renormalizes its action by an amount proportional to $(U-T)^2$, and that it leaves the averaged wiggly string supersonic, its transverse waves faster than its longitudinal ones [carter1999].¶Light crossing the averaged field in the plane normal to the string feels only the conical deficit, and massive particles feel the Newtonian attraction as well [pogosianvachaspati1999]. Andrés Arazi and Claudio Simeone found in 2000 that light moving partly along the string stays between two radii from the axis [arazisimeone2000bransdicke]. Sergei Dyda and Brandenberger traced light past the averaged string in 2007 and found a deflection that depends on where the source lies, which gives nearly round background galaxies a small elongation along the projected string [dydabrandenberger2007]. Frankbelson dos Santos Azevedo and coauthors showed in 2017 that a scalar wave travelling along the string obeys the equation of the hydrogen atom in two dimensions, so the geometry guides a finite number of quantized modes [azevedo2017waveguide]. Azevedo and Edilberto O. Silva added a screw dislocation to the geometry in 2024, and the bound orbits and wave modes then depend on the direction of travel along the string [azevedosilva2024].¶Mark Hindmarsh and Andrew Wray showed in 1990 that beyond the weak field a static cylindrical source has a zero width limit only when its exterior is conical [hindmarshwray1990]. Arazi and Simeone proved in 2000 that a thick cylinder carrying only this energy and tension has no static interior in general relativity when $U\neq T$ [arazisimeone2000cylindrical]. An exact exterior exists once the source also carries equal radial and azimuthal stresses, which can be tied to a current along the axis [ozdemir2001]. Arazi and Simeone also found the averaged field in linearized Brans-Dicke gravity, where the plane normal to the string stays conformal to a cone whose deficit does not depend on the coupling [arazisimeone2000bransdicke]. M. Haluk Seçuk and Özgür Delice found the averaged field in linearized Horndeski gravity, where a massive scalar field is screened far from the string [secukdelice2026]. They also found stable circular orbits about the averaged string for $U>T$, in general relativity as well [secukdelice2026].¶Joan Camps and Roberto Emparan related this field to the static cylindrical vacuum family in 2010 [campsemparan2010]. In their notation its Levi-Civita parameter is $m=2(U-T)$ and its conicity parameter is $C=1+4T$, both through first order. The mass parameter of the Weyl form, $\sigma=m/2$, is therefore $\sigma=U-T$ to this order. The transverse spatial field also depends on the sum $U+T$, so the energy and tension enter the geometry in two combinations. A cylindrical shell sourcing this field carries a hoop stress, which enters only at second order in $m$ [campsemparan2010]. Camps and Emparan used strings of this kind to pull black holes into uniform acceleration, a generalization of the C-metric [campsemparan2010].

related.text: For $U=T$, the Newtonian attraction vanishes and the field reduces to the straight string's conical geometry through first order [campsemparan2010].
A travelling wave retains its dependence on position along the string and time [garfinkle1990]. The averaged wiggly string has a static cylindrical field [campsemparan2010].
The weak field belongs to this cylindrical family, with $\sigma=U-T$ and $C=1+4T$ through first order in units $G=c=1$ [campsemparan2010].

parameters.description: Energy per length of the averaged string, in geometrical units; $U\ge T>0$.
Tension of the averaged string; $UT=\mu_0^2$, where $\mu_0$ is the energy per length and tension of the unperturbed string.
Reference length in the logarithmic potential.

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t,r,\phi,z)$, with $t$, $r$, and $z$ measured as lengths and $\phi$ an angle, and $r_0$ is a positive reference length.
